scope: Original short summaries of common IFAB rules, not the complete Laws or competition regulations. No match evidence or evaluation answers. Rules can change; this is an offline reference, not live web search.

entries.summary: Each team has at most eleven players, including a goalkeeper. A match normally cannot start or continue with fewer than seven; protocols have specific temporary-absence exceptions. Substitution limits depend on competition rules, so do not infer a particular competition's allowance from the general Laws. A player sent off after kick-off cannot be replaced.

entries.topic: Halves, added time and extra time
entries.summary: A standard match has two 45-minute halves. The referee adds time for stoppages such as injuries, substitutions and disciplinary delays. The displayed added time is a minimum and can increase. Half-time is at most fifteen minutes under the usual rules. Added time within a half is different from extra time used by some competitions to resolve a draw.

The entire ball must cross a boundary line to be out, whether airborne or on the ground. Play also stops when the referee stops it. A rebound from the frame of the goal or a corner flag normally remains in play. Contact with an official requires a dropped ball in specified situations, such as a change of possession or the start of a promising attack.

A valid goal requires the whole ball to cross the goal line within the goal, without an offence by the scoring team. The higher final goal total wins; equal totals mean a draw unless competition rules require a tiebreak. Extra time and shoot-outs depend on those rules. A score while play continues establishes the current lead, not the final winner.

Assess relevant head, body or feet position when a teammate plays or touches the ball: the attacker must be in the opponents' half and ahead of both the ball and the second-last opponent. Hands and arms do not count; level is onside. Position alone is not an offence: subsequent involvement must interfere with play or an opponent, or gain the specified advantage from a rebound, deflection or save. The ball's travel direction is not a requirement. Direct reception from a throw-in, corner or goal kick is exempt. A deliberate opponent play generally resets the situation; a deliberate save does not. An offence leads to an indirect free kick.

For physical challenges, careless conduct can be a foul without a card, recklessness calls for a caution, and excessive force can require sending off. Yellow means caution; red means sending off, including a second caution in the same match. Hand contact is not automatically handball: intent, body position and the scoring circumstances matter. A direct-free-kick offence inside the offender's own penalty area normally results in a penalty. A goalkeeper holding the ball with hands or arms beyond eight seconds concedes a corner under this edition.

A direct free kick can score straight into the opponents' goal. An indirect free kick needs another player's touch before a goal can count; the referee signals it with a raised arm. The restart type follows the offence, rather than whether the kicker chooses to pass or shoot.

When the whole ball crosses the touchline, the opponents of its last toucher normally take the throw-in. A legal throw uses both hands from behind and over the head while facing the pitch, with part of each foot on the line or outside it on the ground. A goal cannot be scored straight from a throw-in.

A goal kick normally follows a ball crossing the defending goal line outside a valid goal after an attacker touched it last. It is taken from the goal area. The ball is live once kicked and clearly moving; it need not leave the penalty area first.

A corner normally follows the ball crossing a team's goal line without a goal after a defender touched it last. It is taken from the nearer corner area and can score directly against the opposing team. This edition also awards a corner for excessive goalkeeper hand control and specified goal-kick delay offences.
